topic: Microsoft ASSERT: Turn Agent Policies Into Executable Evaluations (Open-Source Framework Guide)

key_points: Microsoft Responsible AI positions ASSERT, Adaptive Spec-driven Scoring for Evaluation and Regression Testing, as an open-source framework that converts natural-language behavior specifications into executable evaluations.
The article explains the core pipeline: written requirements become test scenarios, datasets, metrics, scorecards, and runnable evaluations against models, apps, or agents.
It frames ASSERT as a bridge between product requirements, policy documents, system prompts, launch checklists, and repeatable evaluation suites.
Microsoft Foundry presents ASSERT as part of an open trust stack alongside Agent Control Specification, with ASSERT handling evaluation and ACS handling runtime controls.
ASSERT is described as requirements-driven, safety-focused, open source, and framework-agnostic across ecosystems such as LangChain, CrewAI, LiteLLM, OpenAI, and related tools.
The article emphasizes a practical loop: run ASSERT to find defects, apply controls, then re-run ASSERT to validate improvement with before-and-after metrics.
The GitHub repo describes ASSERT as a requirement-driven evaluation harness for AI agents and LLM applications.

The project focuses on behavior-specific test case generation, running tests against hosted models, callable wrappers, and OpenTelemetry/OpenInference-traced agents, and inspecting local-first artifacts.
Repo messaging highlights framework independence, including LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, DSPy, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, custom multi-agent orchestration, Python callables, and hosted models.

TechCrunch summarizes the developer value proposition: plain-language AI behavior and policy descriptions become structured acceptable and unacceptable behaviors, scenarios, test cases, execution, and scoring.
The coverage highlights traceability: ASSERT can record intermediate actions and tool calls so developers can inspect where failures happen.
The angle is accessibility for developers who need behavior tests without hand-authoring every evaluation case.
LiteLLM announces support for running ASSERT evaluations through the LiteLLM AI Gateway across 100+ LLM providers.
The partner framing stresses the production gap between demo behavior and policy-compliant behavior under real organizational requirements.
Useful implementation angle: ASSERT can be introduced without standardizing on one model provider, which matters for teams already routing traffic through an AI gateway.
Arize explains how ASSERT, ACS, and observability can share the OpenInference trace contract.
The article frames ASSERT as reading OpenInference spans from an agent as evidence for evaluation judges, while ACS emits policy-control decisions as spans.
Unique angle for the guide: evaluation, policy enforcement, and production observability can be connected through the same telemetry substrate.

stats.fact: Microsoft says ASSERT is designed for the broad ecosystem of roughly 6 million to 13 million generative AI developers, not only Microsoft Foundry users.
Databricks reports that companies using evaluation tools get nearly 6x more AI projects into production, while those using AI governance get over 12x more into production.
Databricks reports that multi-agent architectures grew by 327% in less than four months in its 2026 State of AI Agents research.
OWASP describes its Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 as a globally peer-reviewed framework developed with more than 100 industry experts, researchers, and practitioners.
Microsoft says the open-source Agent Governance Toolkit addresses all 10 OWASP agentic AI risks with deterministic, sub-millisecond policy enforcement.

A June 2026 IBM survey of 2,000 CIOs and CTOs, summarized by ITPro, found that only 11% felt fully prepared for large-scale AI deployment and 77% said their current governance frameworks were inadequate.
The same IBM survey summary says organizations reported an average of 54 AI-related incidents in the prior year, with 17% classified as severe.
Forrester research summarized by ITPro says about 75% of enterprise leaders report adopting agentic AI, but many initiatives remain in pilot mode because of governance, orchestration, and trust gaps.

angles: Position ASSERT as policy-as-evaluation for AI agents: the key shift is not another benchmark, but converting an organization's own written requirements into regression tests.

Explain ASSERT in the context of the Microsoft open trust stack: ASSERT finds policy failures, ACS enforces runtime controls, and OpenInference/OpenTelemetry connects evaluation evidence to production traces.

Show a practical lifecycle for developers: collect policies, turn them into ASSERT specs, generate scenarios, run against the agent, inspect traces and scorecards, patch prompts/tools/controls, then run in CI.
Contrast generic LLM benchmarks with requirement-driven agent tests that check tool use, multi-step behavior, refusal boundaries, escalation paths, and policy compliance.
Make the guide framework-neutral: cover how ASSERT fits teams using LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, LiteLLM, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, custom Python callables, and hosted models.
Use the governance statistics to argue that evaluation and governance are production infrastructure, not optional responsible-AI paperwork.
Include a clear limitations section: generated tests still need review, judge models can be wrong, policies must be specific, and evaluation should be paired with runtime controls and observability.
Give readers a starter checklist for turning a policy paragraph into measurable agent behavior, including positive cases, negative cases, edge cases, telemetry evidence, and pass/fail thresholds.
